docs.text: Press the play button of the panel to play the animation on the molecular view. You can also check the state at any point in time by dragging the current position on the timeline, or by typing a time into the current time field and pressing Enter.

docs.title: 5. Add a camera motion
docs.text:
The view moves smoothly to a saved camera. This is used for effects such as zooming from the overall view to a region of interest.

  1. Set the molecular view to the viewpoint you want as the start, and press New camera from view in the View > Camera panel of the left side panel to save it (→ Camera)
  2. In the same way, set the view to the viewpoint you want as the end and save another camera
  3. In the header of the timeline, set the start camera to the camera for the start point
  4. Choose Camera motion from the add menu
  5. Select the added strip and specify the end camera in Target camera of the inspector (→ CamMotion)

On playback, the view is interpolated from the start camera to the end camera over the span of the strip. If a start camera is specified, the animation always starts from the viewpoint of that camera, regardless of the viewpoint at the time you press play. To add acceleration and deceleration to the viewpoint movement, set the common property Quadric (→ Animation).

docs.title: 6. Add a display switch
docs.text:
This is a display switch such as making the ballstick of a ligand appear partway through. Show / Hide are animations in which a Renderer gradually fades in / fades out over the span of the strip.

  1. Choose Show (fade in) or Hide (fade out) from the add menu
  2. In the inspector, choose the target Renderer from the checklist (→ Show / Hide)

There are also Slide in / Slide out, which bring objects in and out with a movement from off-screen (→ SlideInOutAnim). To leave a span with no elements placed, secure the length with the do-nothing No operation element.

docs.title: 7. Add morphing
docs.text: Morphing animates a structural change by linearly interpolating the coordinates of corresponding atoms between two structures of the same molecule. Here, the structural change between the GTP-bound form (1TND) and the GDP-bound form (1TAG) of transducin-α is used as an example.

docs.title: Load the two structures
docs.text:
1. Choose File > New Tab and create a new scene with New Scene
  2. Fetch 1TND with File > Get PDB.... On the Renderer specification screen, choose trace and specify c; A in Selection (1TND contains three copies of the same molecule (chains A / B / C), so only chain A is displayed)
  3. In the same way, fetch 1TAG with File > Get PDB... (Renderer is trace. It has only chain A, so no Selection is needed)

docs.title: Superpose 1TAG onto 1TND
docs.text:
The two structures are almost the same as molecules, but the positions of the molecules contained in the PDB entries differ. Because morphing interpolation uses the coordinates as they are, superpose the two first.

  1. Open Tools > Molecular superposition...
  2. Choose SSM in Method under Algorithm
  3. Choose 1TND in Molecule under Reference and specify c; A in Selection
  4. Choose 1TAG in Molecule under Moving
  5. Press OK, and 1TAG moves to a position where it overlaps chain A of 1TND

The result of the superposition (RMSD and the number of aligned residues) can be checked in the log of Output in the bottom panel. Note that SSM superposes by matching secondary structures, so it can be used only for proteins.

docs.title: Convert to MorphMol and add a frame
docs.text:
1. Open Tools > Mol morphing animation...
  2. In Target, choose 1TND, the starting point of the change
  3. Press Convert to MorphMol. The molecule is converted to a MorphMol, which can hold multiple frames (structures)
  4. Press Add mol... and choose 1TAG, the end point of the change. The coordinates are copied as a frame
  5. Confirm that the frame list shows the original structure ((this)) and the added structure, then close the dialog

The 1TAG Object that was the copy source is no longer needed, so you can delete it or hide it in the scene tree.

docs.title: Place it on the timeline and play
docs.text:
1. Choose Mol morphing from the add menu of the Animation panel
  2. Select the added strip and specify the converted 1TND in Target MorphMol of the inspector (→ MolAnim)
  3. On playback, the molecule deforms between the GTP-bound form and the GDP-bound form

Chains B and C, ligands and water molecules that exist only on the 1TND side have no correspondence, so they stay still, but they are not visible because only the trace of chain A is displayed.

To make a back-and-forth loop

Add another Mol morphing strip after the first, and set Start value to 1 and End value to 0 in the inspector to get the change in the reverse direction. Placing the two side by side gives a "there and back" loop animation (→ MolAnim).

To create morphing with your own structures

Atoms are matched between frames by chain name, residue number and atom name (the order of atoms in the file does not matter). Failure to match is not an error: atoms present only in the original structure ((this)) stay still, and atoms present only in the added structure are ignored. To deform the whole molecule cleanly, prepare structures with water, ligands, hydrogens, etc. removed and with consistent chain names and residue numbers. Also, linear interpolation is a method suited to representing local structural changes. For large domain motions, create intermediate structures with other software and insert them as frames to make the transition natural.

Differences from CueMol2

In CueMol2, choosing the menu displayed a prompt to select the target and implicitly converted it to a MorphMol. In CueMol3, the target is chosen in Target in the dialog and converted explicitly with the Convert to MorphMol button (this can be undone with Undo).

docs.title: 8. Export as a movie
docs.text:
Choose Rendering > Movie rendering... and the rendering window opens in Movie mode (→ Rendering window).

  1. Choose the target view in Target. Backend can be left at the default Umbreon
  2. Choose the size in the Image tab (e.g. HD1080 (1920×1080))
  3. Press Start Render. The frames are rendered one by one, and when finished they are encoded into a movie file with ffmpeg (bundled with the macOS / Windows release assets; → Configuring external tools)
  4. By default the output is created in a temporary folder. Use Save movie as... to save the finished movie wherever you like

A Frame rate of 24 to 30 is usually sufficient. Movie rendering takes "number of frames × time per still image", so it is safest to try the size and quality on a single still image first. For presentations, a size around VGA / SVGA is enough. Output settings such as the frame rate and movie format are remembered next time. The settings for raising quality are shared with still images (→ Exporting high-resolution images for publication).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Animation — element types and common properties
  • Rendering window — settings of the movie mode
  • Camera — saving viewpoints and display flags

Verified against: CueMol3 2.4.0.546

docs.title: Overlaying an electron density map
docs.text:
This tutorial shows how to overlay an electron density map on an X-ray crystal structure and check how the model fits the density. The example is the crystal structure of lysozyme (PDB ID: 1QIO); the 2Fo-Fc map and the Fo-Fc map are downloaded from the network together with the coordinates.

Screenshots planned

Screenshots showing the workflow will be added to this page.

docs.title: 1. Fetch the coordinates and density maps together
docs.text:
File > Get PDB... can fetch electron density maps in addition to coordinates.

  1. Enter 1QIO in PDB Accession Code
  2. In addition to Fetch coord file, check Fetch 2Fo-Fc map and Fetch Fo-Fc map
  3. Leave the map source at the default RCSB (cif.gz) (EBI (MTZ) also works)
  4. When the download finishes, a dialog appears for specifying the Object name and Renderer of the coordinates. Choosing simple (line drawing) here makes it easier to see the correspondence between density and atoms

No Renderer dialog appears for the maps; they are displayed automatically with the following configuration.

Object Renderer Color Level 1qio_2fofc contour1 Blue +1.0σ 1qio_fofc pos-cont Green +3.0σ 1qio_fofc neg-cont Red −3.0σ

The 2Fo-Fc map (blue) is the density that envelops the whole model. The Fo-Fc map shows the difference between the observed data and the model: green indicates places where there is density but no model, and red indicates places where there is a model but no density.

docs.title: 2. Check the display
docs.text:
In the Explorer > Scene tree in the left side panel (scene tree → Side panels), the map Objects (1qio_2fofc / 1qio_fofc) and their contour Renderers are listed separately from the coordinate Object. The eye icons toggle their visibility individually.

Crystallographic maps are drawn only around the view center. When the molecular view is translated, the displayed map region follows (a cryo-EM map is drawn in its entirety, and the display range adjustment below is not needed → Region in contour).

The name "contour" comes from extending the familiar two-dimensional contour lines of maps to three dimensions. For how the display works, see contour; for the map Object, see DensityMap.

docs.title: 3. Adjust the level and extent
docs.text:
The map display is adjusted in the Crystal > Density map panel in the left side panel (→ Side panels).

  1. At the top, select the target Renderer (such as 1qio_2fofc/contour1)
  2. Change the contour level with the Level slider. Raise it when noise is distracting, and lower it to see weak density
  3. Change the display range (distance from the center) with the Extent slider
  4. Change the transparency with the Transp slider

By default, the level of a crystallographic map is in σ units (the standard deviation of the map taken as 1). As a guide, view the 2Fo-Fc map at 1 to 1.5σ and the Fo-Fc map at around ±3σ. The ▼ menu item Use absolute contour level switches to specifying an absolute value (the value in the other unit is shown below Level). For a cryo-EM map, the unit is the top percentage of grid point values instead of σ, and the level is specified as an absolute value when the map is loaded. Note that the upper limit of Extent is determined by the Buffer size property of the contour; to extend it further, increase it in the inspector.

docs.title: 4. Focus on a region of interest
docs.text:
This is the procedure for zooming in on a region of interest such as the active site.

  1. Move the view in the molecular view so that the region of interest is at the center
  2. Lower Extent to about 10 Å to reduce the surrounding mesh
  3. If the display has not followed, Redraw in the panel updates the display center to the current view center
  4. Narrowing the Slab (the width of the depth range displayed) also reduces the mesh in front of and behind the region of interest, making it easier to see (→ the View panel in Side panels)

To see only the green and red Fo-Fc meshes, close the eye icon of 1qio_2fofc in the scene tree to hide the 2Fo-Fc map temporarily.

docs.title: 5. Finish as a figure
docs.text: A figure containing a density map can be exported in the same way as an ordinary scene (→ Exporting high-resolution images for publication).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Displaying symmetry mates and the unit cell — look at the crystal packing of the same 1QIO
  • contour / DensityMap — details of the display settings
  • Side panels — each item of the Density map panel

Verified against: CueMol3 2.3.13.523

docs.title: Exporting high-resolution images for publication
docs.text:
This tutorial walks through exporting a scene as an image of publication or presentation quality. It uses the scene finished in Making a protein ribbon figure as the example, but the procedure is the same for any scene.

Screenshots planned

Screenshots showing the workflow will be added to this page.

docs.title: 1. The two output methods and when to use them
docs.text:
Method Characteristics Suited for Rendering > Export scene > PNG image... Exports the on-screen rendering as is. Fast Working records, slides, checking Rendering > Image rendering... (rendering window) High-quality rendering by ray tracing. Higher quality shading and outlines Figures for papers, posters

A quick and reliable workflow is to check the composition with Export scene first, then finish the final version in the rendering window. The finished image is normally pasted into presentation software or figure-making software to assemble a composite figure.

docs.title: 2. Exporting the screen as PNG
docs.text:
When Rendering > Export scene > PNG image... is selected, an options screen appears after the destination is specified.

  • Size and resolution (DPI) can be specified
  • Enabling background transparency produces a PNG with a transparent background (useful for overlaying on slides)

DPI does not affect the number of pixels in the image. It determines the physical size on paper when the exported PNG is pasted into other software and printed (for example, a 1200×1200 pixel image exported at 600 DPI prints at 2×2 inches, about 5 cm square).

For other output formats (POV-Ray SDL / STL / MQO, etc.), see the Rendering menu.

docs.title: 3. Finishing with ray tracing
docs.text:
When Rendering > Image rendering... is selected, a separate rendering window opens in Still mode. The window is modeless, so the view can be adjusted in the main window while it stays open (→ Rendering window).

  1. In the run bar at the bottom, select the view to render in Target. Backend can be left at the default, Umbreon
  2. Select the output size in the Image tab. Choose a preset (for example, 1200×1200 (600dpi)) or specify the width and height directly with Custom
  3. In the Quality section of the Render tab, set Lighting (how shading is applied) to Raytrace only. This is sufficient to give a clean result for a cartoon figure like this one. Supersampling (the setting that smooths outlines) can be left at the default
  4. Press Start Render to start rendering. Progress is displayed

Global Illumination for depth in shading

Setting Lighting to Global Illumination (the default) gives shading by global illumination, which adds a sense of depth. For figures with only a cartoon, however, the effect is small. Try it on figures with intricate shapes such as molecular surfaces.

For the meaning of each quality item and how to choose among them, see Rendering.

Differences from CueMol2

High-quality output in CueMol2 called an external POV-Ray, but in CueMol3 the built-in ray tracer Umbreon is the default, and neither preparing an external program nor setting a path is needed (→ Rendering window).

docs.title: 4. Checking and saving the result
docs.text:
When rendering completes, the resulting image is displayed in the image area at the upper left of the window.

  • Save in the image area toolbar saves it as a PNG file
  • Copy copies it to the clipboard
  • The arrow buttons step back through the history of past rendering results. The history also records the settings used at the time, and pressing Use settings restores them

If the composition or quality is not satisfactory, adjust in the main window and run Start Render again. Settings remain in the result history, so results can be compared while experimenting.

Rendering window settings are saved in the scene

The settings are saved together with the scene file and are still there the next time the scene is opened. Changes to the settings can be reverted with Undo. To return to past settings, use Use settings in the result history (→ Rendering).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Rendering — Details and default values of the quality items
  • Rendering window — Description of each part of the window

Verified against: CueMol3 2.3.13.523

docs.title: Making a protein ribbon figure
docs.text:
This tutorial follows the whole process of building a single figure: display a protein as a cartoon (a so-called ribbon diagram), overlay a ligand as a ballstick, and finish the figure by adjusting colors and outlines. The example is the crystal structure of channelrhodopsin (PDB ID: 3UG9).

This tutorial assumes you have gone through the Quick tour (startup, loading, and basic view operations).

Screenshots planned

Screenshots showing the workflow will be added to this page.

docs.title: 1. Fetch the structure
docs.text:
Use File > Get PDB... to fetch the structure from the network.

  1. Enter 3UG9 in PDB Accession Code
  2. Make sure Fetch coord file is checked (leave the format at the default, RCSB (mmCIF))
  3. When the download finishes, a screen for specifying the Object name and Renderer appears
  4. Select cartoon from Renderer type, and create it with everything else at the defaults

The protein part is drawn as a cartoon that reflects the secondary structure (→ cartoon).

A preset does it in one step

If you select Default preset 2 under Presets in Renderer type, a Renderer group is created at once, combining a cartoon for the protein, a ballstick for nucleic acids, and a ballstick for everything else (ligands and so on). In this tutorial, Renderers are created one by one to show how it works.

docs.title: 2. Adjust the view
docs.text:
Rotate with a left drag on the molecular view and zoom with the wheel until the whole molecule is visible (→ Mouse and trackpad input).

To fit the view to the whole molecule again, select the Object (3UG9) in the Explorer > Scene tree of the left side panel (the scene tree → Side panels), and press the Focus button at the top of the panel.

docs.title: 3. Adjust the appearance of the cartoon
docs.text:
When you select the cartoon Renderer in the scene tree, its settings appear in the property inspector on the right. Changes are reflected in the molecular view immediately and can be undone with Cmd+Z / Ctrl+Z.

The width and thickness of helices are adjusted in the Helix section, those of sheets in Sheet, and those of loops in Coil. For example, if the ligand overlaid in a later step is hard to see because it is hidden by a helix, making the Helix width thinner lets you see inside. For the meaning and default of each property, see cartoon.

docs.title: 4. Color each domain differently
docs.text:
3UG9 contains a single molecule (chain A). Three regions, the N-terminal domain, the transmembrane part, and the C-terminal domain, are colored separately by residue number range.

  1. Open the Explorer > Color panel in the left side panel
  2. Select the cartoon Renderer at the top
  3. Select Paint as the Coloring type
  4. Create the following three rows in the table and specify a color of your choice for each
Region Selection expression N-terminal domain A.49:83.* Transmembrane part A.84:317.* C-terminal domain A.318:342.*

Paint is evaluated from the top row down, and the color of the first matching row is used (→ Coloring). A.49:83.* means "all atoms of residues 49 to 83 in chain A" (→ Selection expression syntax).

Differences from CueMol2

CueMol2 also had a Paint panel, but rows (entries) had to be edited in a separate dialog. In CueMol3, table cells can be edited directly (→ Merged, renamed, and removed features).

For a single chain, Rainbow is also a classic

Rainbow, which changes color like a rainbow from the N terminus to the C terminus, is also a classic way to show the course of the chain. Just select Rainbow as the Coloring type to apply it.

Styles can keep colors consistent across figures

Giving names to color and selection definitions and sharing them lets you make figures with a consistent color scheme across multiple scenes (→ Styles).

docs.title: 5. Show the ligand as a ballstick
docs.text:
A cartoon draws only the course of the main chain, so the ligand is not displayed. Overlay the retinal (residue name RET) of 3UG9 as a ballstick (ball-and-stick model).

  1. Right-click the Object (3UG9) in the scene tree and select New Renderer
  2. Select ballstick from Renderer type
  3. Check Selection and enter r; RET as the selection expression
  4. Press Create, and the retinal is drawn as a ballstick over the cartoon

Multiple Renderers can be stacked on one Object in this way. What each Renderer displays is narrowed down with a selection expression (r; is a shorthand for selection by residue name → Selection expression syntax).

If you do not know the residue name, you can also find and select the residue in the tree of the Selection > Molecular structure panel (→ Side panels). If the ligand is too small to see in an overview figure, displaying it as cpk (space-filling model) instead of ballstick is also a classic choice.

docs.title: 6. Finish with a background and outlines
docs.text:
In figures for papers, combining a white background with outlines (edge lines) is a classic choice. Edge lines make the boundaries of each element clear even on a white background.

  1. Set the background to white with Scene > Background > White
  2. Right-click the cartoon Renderer in the scene tree
  3. Select Style > Edge line (normal). The edge line type and width are set together
  4. Repeat the same operation (steps 2-3) for the ballstick Renderer

To make the lines thicker or thinner, select Edge line (thick) / Edge line (thin) from the same menu. To remove them, select No edge line (→ Edge lines).

Check the ligand colors on a white background

On a white background, light-colored atoms may blend into the background and become hard to see. If this bothers you, darken the carbon color with CPK in the Color panel (for example #404040) (→ Color syntax).

docs.title: 7. Save the camera and scene
docs.text:
Once the view is decided, save it as a camera so that you can return to the same composition later.

  1. Click View in the activity bar to open the Camera panel
  2. Press the New camera from view button, and create a camera with a name

Double-clicking a camera row returns to that view at any time (→ Camera).

Finally, save the scene to a .qsc file with File > Save Scene (Cmd+S / Ctrl+S). On saving, the current view is also recorded as a camera named __current and is applied the next time the file is opened. If you enable data embedding in the save options, the molecular data is also included in the .qsc, so the file can be carried around by itself (→ File menu).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Exporting high-resolution images for publication — finish this figure by ray tracing
  • Coloring / Selection expression syntax — details of coloring and selection
  • Renderer list — learn about other display methods

Verified against: CueMol3 2.3.15.530

docs.title: Coloring a molecular surface by electrostatic potential
Coloring a molecular surface by electrostatic potential
docs.text:
This tutorial generates a molecular surface, colors it by the electrostatic potential calculated with APBS, and produces a figure showing the charge distribution of the molecule. The example is lysozyme (PDB ID: 1QIO). It is a basic protein, so the positively charged regions of its surface stand out clearly.

Screenshots planned

Screenshots showing the workflow will be added to this page.

docs.title: 1. Load the structure
docs.text: Fetch 1QIO with File > Get PDB... (coordinates only is fine). Select cartoon as the Renderer.

docs.title: 2. Generate the molecular surface
docs.text:
Open Tools > Mol surface generation....

  1. Select 1QIO in Molecule under Target
  2. Enable Use selection and enter protein as the selection expression. Crystal structures contain water molecules, and without this the surface would be calculated around the waters as well
  3. Raise Point density (/A) to 5. This sets the fineness of the surface, and raising it gives a smoother surface for a small protein such as 1QIO (for very large molecules, the default of 2 is faster)
  4. Object name and Probe radius (A) (1.4 Å, the radius of a water molecule) can be left at their defaults
  5. Algorithm can also be left at the default Auto (→ MolSurfObj (molecular surface))
  6. Click OK. A molecular surface Object and a molsurf Renderer are created, and the surface is displayed

The MolSurf Object holds only the shape of the surface. The molsurf Renderer refers to the molecule specified in Selection mol in the inspector (here, 1QIO, from which the surface was generated) for coloring and selection. To display only part of the surface, specify the range in Selection. For details, see MolSurf / molsurf.

docs.title: 3. Calculate the electrostatic potential
docs.text:
Open Tools > APBS elepot calculation....

  1. Select 1QIO in Molecule under Target
  2. Enable Use selection here as well and enter protein (the calculation is normally done without water and ions)
  3. Elepot name (the name of the electrostatic potential map Object to be created) can be left at the default
  4. Leave Method under Charge method at the default Use PDB2PQR
  5. Click Start. The calculation runs in the order pdb2pqr, then apbs, and the progress is displayed. It takes time for large molecules. When it finishes, an electrostatic potential map (ElePotMap) Object is added to the scene

APBS and pdb2pqr are bundled with the macOS / Windows release assets, so installation and configuration are normally not needed. For builds that do not bundle them (such as Linux), install them separately and specify the paths in Settings (→ Configuring external tools).

Calculation conditions such as temperature and dielectric constants can be changed in APBS options. A box showing the region over which the map was calculated (a *unitcell Renderer) is also added to the scene. Once you have confirmed that the region is large enough, you can hide it. For details on the electrostatic potential map Object, see ElePotMap.

docs.title: 4. Color the surface by electrostatic potential
docs.text:
1. Open the Explorer > Color panel in the left side panel
  2. Select the molsurf Renderer at the top
  3. Select Electrostatic potential as the Coloring type
  4. In Potential, select the electrostatic potential map created in step 3
  5. Enable By SAS. The values on the surface itself (SES) are too close to the charged atoms and tend to give a mottled coloring, so the surface is colored with the values on the solvent-accessible surface (SAS), which lies outside the surface by the radius of a water molecule (1.4 Å)
  6. Set High to about 2 and Low to about -2. The unit of the values is kT/e, and with the default of ±10 hardly any color appears. The narrower the range, the stronger the contrast

For details on the settings, see Coloring.

docs.title: 5. Overlay a translucent surface and the cartoon
docs.text:
To show the structure inside the surface as well, make the surface translucent and overlay it on the cartoon.

  1. Select the molsurf Renderer in the Explorer > Scene tree (scene tree) in the left side panel
  2. In the Common section of the property inspector, lower Opacity to about 0.5

This gives the classic overlay in which the path of the main chain is visible through the surface. For finishing and export, see Exporting high-resolution images for publication.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Exporting high-resolution images for publication — finish this figure by ray tracing
  • Coloring — settings for electrostatic potential
  • MolSurf / ElePotMap — details of the generated Objects

Verified against: CueMol3 2.4.0.546

docs.title: Displaying symmetry mates and the unit cell
Displaying symmetry mates and the unit cell
docs.text:
This tutorial shows how to display the neighboring molecules generated by crystal symmetry operations (symmetry mates) and the unit cell frame, in order to check crystal packing. The example is the same lysozyme structure (PDB ID: 1QIO) as in the previous tutorial. You can also follow it as a continuation of Overlaying an electron density map.

Screenshots planned

Screenshots showing the workflow will be added to this page.

docs.title: 1. Load the crystal structure
docs.text: Fetch 1QIO with File > Get PDB... (coordinates only is fine). Choose a Renderer that shows the outline of the molecule, such as cartoon.

docs.title: 2. Check the crystallographic information
docs.text:
Open the Crystal > Symmetry panel in the left side panel (→ Side panels).

  1. Select the target (1QIO) in Object
  2. The cell parameters (a / b / c / α / β / γ) and the space group are displayed

Structures fetched from the PDB contain crystallographic information, so you can usually go straight to the next step.

If the displayed values differ from the actual ones

Depending on the PDB file, the values shown here may differ from what was intended. In that case, or when you load a file without symmetry information, the crystal system and space group can be set again with Change... in the panel (→ Side panels).

docs.title: 3. Display the unit cell
docs.text: Click the Unit cell button in the panel to add the unit cell frame to the scene. It appears in the Explorer > Scene tree (scene tree) in the left side panel as a Renderer named *unitcell, and can be shown or hidden with the eye icon.

docs.title: 4. Display symmetry mates
docs.text:
Choose the display range with the Symm mol button in the panel.

  • 20 Å / 50 Å / 100 Å / 200 Å — Displays the symmetry mates within that distance of the current view center. The display follows automatically when you move the view
  • Unit cell — Displays the symmetry mates for one unit cell

The symmetry mates are added to the scene tree as a Renderer named *symm, drawn with the same display style and colors as the original Renderer. *symm only shows the original Renderer's display transformed by the symmetry operations. Like a mirror image, it has no entity (coordinate data) of its own. However many symmetry mates are displayed, the original Object is unchanged.

The space group of 1QIO, P43212, has 8 symmetry operations, so choosing Unit cell displays 8 molecules per unit cell.

A clear way to work is to first check only the molecules in contact with 20 Å, and switch to Unit cell or a larger distance when looking at the whole packing.

docs.title: 5. Make a symmetry mate an independent Object
docs.text:
One of the displayed symmetry mates can be extracted as an independent Object with its own coordinates. Use this for contact interface analysis or to make a figure in which only the symmetry mate is colored differently.

  1. In the molecular view, right-click an atom of the symmetry mate (with the Navigate tool)
  2. The symmetry operation (symop: ...) is shown at the top of the menu, which confirms that the atom belongs to a symmetry mate
  3. Choose Create SYMM mol...
  4. Specify the name and Renderer type of the new Object and click Create

A new molecular Object with the coordinates after applying the symmetry operation is created. From then on, Renderers can be added and colors set as for any other Object. The operation can be undone with Undo.

With Center at SYMM atom in the same menu, the view center can be moved to the clicked atom of the symmetry mate. The similarly named Center at this atom targets the atom (the entity) before the symmetry operation, so choosing it while looking at a symmetry mate sends the view to a distant location.

docs.title: 6. Adjust or remove the display
docs.text:
• To change the display range, choose again from Symm mol
  • To remove the symmetry mates or the unit cell, delete the *symm / *unitcell Renderer in the scene tree, or hide it with the eye icon

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Overlaying an electron density map — Check the density on the same 1QIO
  • Exporting high-resolution images for publication — Export the packing view
  • Side panels — Each item of the Symmetry panel

Verified against: CueMol3 2.3.8.494

docs.title: Saving the camera and the scene
Saving the camera and the scene
docs.text:
This page shows how to keep a favorite viewpoint as a camera, and how to save the whole working state to a scene file (.qsc) and resume from it. It continues from the previous page (Coloring Renderers).

Screenshots planned

Screenshots showing the workflow will be added to this page.

docs.title: 1. Save a viewpoint as a camera
docs.text:
While examining a molecule, you often want to come back to a particular view later. The position, orientation, zoom and slab of a view can be saved as a named camera.

  1. Set up the view you want to save
  2. Click View in the activity bar and open the Camera panel
  3. Press the New camera from view button at the top of the panel
  4. Give it a name and create it (the default name is fine)

The new camera appears in the list. Move the view around, then double-click the camera row. The saved view is restored.

The right-click menu of a camera row offers renaming, deleting, copy & paste, reading and writing camera files (.cam), editing display flags, and more (→ Camera).

docs.title: 2. Save the scene
docs.text:
The whole scene (Objects, Renderers, colors and cameras) is saved to a .qsc file with File > Save Scene (Cmd+S / Ctrl+S). Save it as tutorial1.qsc here.

When saving, the current view is automatically recorded as a camera named __current. This camera is applied when the scene is opened, so the scene looks exactly as it did when saved.

Links and embedding

For a .qsc file, the save options let you choose whether to store links to the loaded data files or to embed the data itself (→ File menu). With links, the scene cannot be opened if the original files are moved or deleted. Objects that have no original file, such as those fetched from the network, are embedded. Embedding is the safe choice when you want to carry the scene as a single file.

docs.title: 3. Open a scene
docs.text: Quit CueMol3 and start it again, then open tutorial1.qsc with File > Open Scene.... The saved state is restored as it was (it can also be opened from File > Open Recent).

docs.title: 4. Work with multiple scenes in tabs
docs.text:
Each scene corresponds to a tab at the top of the window, and several scenes can be open at once. Scenes are independent and do not affect each other.

  1. Choose File > New Tab (Cmd+T) and create a new scene with New Scene
  2. The new scene is empty, so nothing is displayed
  3. Fetch 1EHZ (a tRNA structure) with File > Get PDB... and choose nucl, the type for nucleic acids, as the Renderer type
  4. Click the tabs to switch between scenes. The contents of the scene tree also switch to the scene of that tab

docs.title: Close a tab
docs.text: Close a scene with the close button of its tab (or File > Close Tab). For a scene with unsaved changes, a confirmation asks whether to save (→ File menu).

docs.title: 5. View the same scene from another viewpoint
docs.text:
If you choose New View in File > New Tab, a tab is created that holds another view of the current scene, instead of a new scene (you can also choose whether to inherit the current camera).

The scene is shared by both tabs, so selection and color changes are reflected in both. The viewpoint, on the other hand, is independent for each view, so you can switch quickly between two ways of looking at the scene. To keep the viewpoint itself, a camera is more suitable than a view (cameras are saved in the scene file).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Measurement and interaction display — measure distances and angles and keep them in a figure
  • Camera / File menu

Verified against: CueMol3 2.3.15.530

docs.title: Coloring Renderers
docs.text:
The color of a Renderer is changed in the Color panel, which handles only the Coloring part of the settings. This page tries the main Coloring types in turn, using lysozyme (simple + ballstick + ribbon) and 1G59 (trace) from the previous page (Adding, removing and configuring Renderers).

Screenshots planned

Screenshots showing the workflow will be added to this page.

docs.title: 1. Using the Color panel
docs.text:
Open the Explorer > Color panel in the left side panel (→ Side panels).

  1. Select the target Renderer at the top (selecting a Renderer in the scene tree also updates this)
  2. Select the Coloring type; the settings for that type appear below

For the list of types and their settings, see Coloring.

docs.title: 2. CPK — color by element
docs.text:
CPK assigns a color to each element, and is the standard choice for simple and ballstick.

  1. Select lysozyme/ballstick1 as the target
  2. Select CPK as the Coloring type
  3. Change the color of C (carbon) to gray (for example, #808080)

Only the carbon parts of the ballstick turn gray. For how to specify colors (color names, color codes, etc.), see Color syntax.

docs.title: 3. B-factor — gradient by value
docs.text:
B-factor changes the color continuously according to values such as the temperature factor.

  1. Select lysozyme/simple1 as the target (if you hid it, restore it with the eye icon)
  2. Select B-factor as the Coloring type

The structure is painted with a gradient from low to high temperature factors. The colors at the lower and upper limits and the value range (Auto / Manual) can also be set.

docs.title: 4. Rainbow — rainbow from end to end
docs.text:
Rainbow changes the hue along the residue sequence.

  1. Select 1G59/trace1 as the target
  2. Select Rainbow as the Coloring type
  3. Switch the mode from whole molecule to per chain

In 1G59 the protein and the tRNA are separate chains, so each is painted with its own rainbow (the protein from the N-terminus to the C-terminus, the RNA from the 5' end to the 3' end).

docs.title: 5. Paint — color by pairs of selection and color
docs.text:
Paint offers the most freedom. Pairs of a "selection expression and a color" are listed as rows of a table, and the rows are evaluated from the top, with the color of the first matching row used for painting.

  1. Select lysozyme/ribbon1 as the target
  2. Select Paint > Default as the Coloring type. A table appears containing the standard secondary-structure coloring (four rows: sheet / helix / nucleic / *)
  3. Rewrite the table as the following three rows (in this order from the top)
Selection expression Example color helix light blue sheet green * whitish

helix and sheet are predefined selections that represent secondary structure (→ Selection expression syntax). The * (everything) row is at the bottom, so only the coil regions, which are neither helix nor sheet, get this color.

docs.title: Add a paint
docs.text:
Change the color of only the C-terminal helix (residues 119 to 129).

  1. Add a row at the top of the table
  2. Specify A.119:129.* as the selection expression and red as the color

The C-terminal region turns red. Because this row is above the helix row, red takes precedence in this range. Layering paints while keeping the row order in mind is how Paint is used. Rows that are no longer needed can be deleted.

Presets are also available

In addition to the Default used above, the Paint submenu lists color schemes prepared as styles (Woody / Red, etc.). Applying a preset first and then rewriting its rows is also a quick approach.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Saving the camera and the scene — keep the viewpoint and working state
  • Coloring / Color syntax

Verified against: CueMol3 2.3.13.523

docs.title: Loading and displaying a structure
docs.text:
This page covers loading and displaying a molecular structure, and the Scene / Object / Renderer concepts at the core of CueMol3. The example is the 1.2 Å resolution crystal structure of lysozyme (PDB ID: 1QIO).

The pages of the basic course carry over the state of the previous page when followed in order.

docs.title: 1. Load a structure
docs.text:
Open File > Get PDB..., enter 1QIO in PDB Accession Code, and download it. To open a local file, use File > Open File... (Cmd+O) (→ File menu).

While downloading, a Downloading 1QIO… progress screen appears. Press Cancel to abort. If a nonexistent ID is entered, a Get PDB failed error is shown.

When the download finishes, the Open File Options screen appears. At the top it shows the name of the file to be loaded (1qio.cif) and the file format CueMol3 detected (mmCIF).

  1. Change Object name to lysozyme. The loaded data is called an Object, and CueMol identifies it by this name (by default, a name derived from the file name is filled in)
  2. Choose simple from Renderer type
  3. Renderer name is set automatically from the chosen type (simple1). Leave it at the default. This name is used as is in the scene tree and in the rest of the tutorial
  4. Leave the other options at their defaults and press Open

The molecule is displayed as a line drawing (stick model).

docs.title: Renderer types
docs.text:
Commonly used display styles include the following.

simple Line-drawing stick model. Second fastest after trace. Suited to viewing details trace Line-drawing Cα trace (for proteins) or phosphorus-atom trace (for nucleic acids). The fastest. Suited to a rough overview ballstick Ball-and-stick model cpk CPK model, also called a space-filling model tube Tube model of the main chain. A kind of extension of trace ribbon / cartoon The so-called ribbon model. cartoon draws helices as cylinders nucl An extension of tube for DNA and RNA. Bases are displayed as sticks

For the full list and details, see Renderer list.

At the top of the Renderer type list there is a group called Presets. Choosing Default preset 1 or similar there creates not a single Renderer but a group of several Renderers at once, for example ribbon for proteins, nucl for nucleic acids, and ballstick for everything else. When a preset is chosen, Selection below becomes unavailable.

docs.title: Other options
docs.text:
• Renderer name — The name of the Renderer to be created. It is filled in automatically when a type is chosen (for a preset, it becomes the group name)
  • Selection — When checked, the adjacent field is enabled and the range to display can be narrowed with a selection expression. Loading itself is performed on the whole molecule, so the displayed range can be changed later (→ Selecting part of a molecule)
  • Center view on molecule after loading — Moves the view to the loaded molecule. Uncheck it to keep the current view
  • <format>-specific options — A collapsible section at the bottom. When opened, it lists the loading settings specific to that format (for mmCIF / PDB, Load MODEL records, Load anisotropic U (ANISOU), Load alternate conformations, Calculate secondary structure, and so on). (defaults) is shown to the right of the heading when the settings are at their defaults, and (modified) when they have been changed

docs.title: 2. Manipulate the view
docs.text:
Look at the loaded molecule from various directions.

  1. Left-drag on the molecular view. The molecule rotates in the direction of the drag
  2. Turn the wheel to zoom the display in and out

  3. In the View > View panel in the left side panel, click the Zoom value under Zoom / Slab, enter 40, and press Enter. Zoom is set to 40

Zoom is the height (Å) of the range shown in the molecular view. The smaller the value, the larger the molecule appears.

Each row of the View panel can be operated in three ways.

  • Press the left/right arrows to increase or decrease the value one step at a time
  • Drag left or right over the number to change it continuously
  • Click the number to make it directly editable, and press Enter to confirm

The View panel is thus useful when the view needs to be set more precisely than is possible with the mouse. Rotation (RotX / RotY / RotZ) values are relative: the view rotates by the entered angle, and the value returns to 0 after the operation. Translation (TraX / TraY / TraZ, Å) and Zoom / Slab (Zoom, Slab, Dist, Å) values are absolute: the values of the current view are displayed as they are.

For the full list of operations, including translation and slab (the range displayed by clipping the near and far sides), see Mouse and trackpad input; for each item of the View panel, see Side panels.

docs.title: Show atom names and information
docs.text:
Click at an atom's position to show the name of that atom in the molecular view (click again to hide it).

Detailed information on the atom, such as its coordinates and temperature factor, is also shown in the status bar at the bottom of the window (the same content remains in the Output panel). It lists the molecular Object name, chain name, residue name and number, and atom name in that order, followed by the occupancy (O), temperature factor (B), and coordinates.

Right-clicking at an atom's position shows a context menu. The top entry shows the same atom information as above; selecting it does nothing. Selecting the next entry, Center at this atom, moves the view so that the atom comes to the center. The Select-related menu items below that are described in Selecting part of a molecule.

docs.title: 3. Load another molecule
docs.text:
Multiple Objects can be loaded into the same scene. Here, add 1G59 (a complex of glutamyl-tRNA synthetase and tRNA).

  1. Open File > Get PDB..., enter 1G59 in PDB Accession Code, and press Download

  2. Choose trace from Renderer type

  3. Leave Object name at the default (1g59) and press Open

This draws a lightweight display connecting only Cα atoms for the protein and phosphorus atoms for the nucleic acid. The asymmetric unit of 1G59 contains two copies of the complex (2 protein chains + 2 tRNA chains), so the same shape appears twice.

After loading, the view moves to the new molecule (Center view on molecule after loading is on by default), so lysozyme is not visible at this point. To see both at once, operate the View panel in the same way as in §2.

  1. Enter 300 in Slab
  2. Enter 150 in Zoom
  3. Enter 90 in RotY

The key is to widen Slab (the thickness displayed along the depth direction). With the default 50 Å, lysozyme, which lies about 100 Å away from 1G59, is clipped by the depth range no matter how far Zoom is widened. Also, the three molecules overlap along the depth direction, so in the loaded orientation they overlap front to back and cannot be told apart. Rotating by 90° with RotY makes them appear side by side.

To view only a particular Object, select its row in the scene tree and press the Focus button at the top of the panel. Zoom and Slab are adjusted automatically to fit that Object.

docs.title: 4. Scene, Object, Renderer and View
docs.text:
This section summarizes the concepts that have appeared so far.

Object Data such as molecular coordinates, electron density, or electrostatic potential. It does not appear on screen by itself Renderer Responsible for displaying an Object on screen. Multiple Renderers can be attached to one Object, so the same molecule can be displayed as ribbon and ballstick at the same time, for example Scene A unit of work that groups Objects and Renderers. The tabs at the top of the window correspond to scenes, and scenes opened side by side do not interfere with each other View The screen that shows a scene (the molecular view). Multiple Views can also be connected to one scene (→ New Tab in the File menu)

Think of a scene as the whole that contains multiple Objects and the Renderers attached to them.

docs.title: 5. Get an overview in the scene tree
docs.text:
The Explorer > Scene tree (scene tree) in the left side panel shows the Objects in the scene and their Renderers in a hierarchy (→ Side panels).

Rows are written as name (type). Click the triangle to the left of a name to expand or collapse the list of Renderers attached to that Object. The current tree reads as follows.

  • The scene Untitled 1 has two Objects, lysozyme and 1g59 (when loaded with Get PDB, the Object name is the lowercase PDB ID)
  • 1g59 (MolCoord) — The type of Object 1g59 is MolCoord (molecular coordinates)
  • trace1 (trace) — The Renderer trace1 attached to 1g59 is of type trace
  • (*selection) — A Renderer without a name is shown with only parentheses and its type. This is the Renderer for highlighting the selected part, and it is created automatically when a molecule is loaded
  • (*namelabel) — The Renderer for labels, created when an atom was clicked to show its name in §2. The row remains even after the label is hidden

Camera and Styles at the bottom are the places where saved views and styles are kept (→ Saving the camera and the scene).

docs.title: Eye icons and buttons at the top of the panel
docs.text:
• The eye icon on a row toggles the visibility of a Renderer. Toggling it on an Object row toggles all Renderers under it together
  • There are four buttons at the top of the panel (names appear when the pointer is placed over them)
Button Action Add Adds a Renderer to the selected Object (same as New Renderer in the right-click menu) Focus Adjusts the view (Zoom and Slab) to fit the selected Object or Renderer Delete Deletes the selected Object or Renderer. It can be restored with Undo Property Shows the selected item in the property inspector

Right-clicking the scene row lets you change the background color from Background color.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Selecting part of a molecule — How to choose what to operate on
  • Mouse and trackpad input / Side panels

Verified against: CueMol3 2.3.8.495

docs.title: Measurement and interaction display
docs.text:
This tutorial shows how to measure distances, angles and dihedral angles between atoms, and how to adjust their display as part of a figure. The example is again lysozyme (lysozyme, simple display).

Screenshots planned

Screenshots showing the workflow will be added to this page.

docs.title: 1. Measure distances
docs.text:
Measurements use the Measure group in the tool palette at the left edge of the molecular view (→ Toolbar and tool palette).

  1. Select the Distance tool in the tool palette (shortcut D)
  2. Click the first atom of the distance to measure. A cross mark shows the progress
  3. Click the second atom. A dotted line is drawn between the atoms and a distance label is shown

Keep clicking to measure several distances in succession. To stop partway, press Esc or switch to another tool such as Navigate.

docs.title: 2. Measure angles and dihedral angles
docs.text:
• Angle tool (A) — click three atoms in order to display their angle
  • Torsion tool (T) — click four atoms in order to display their dihedral angle

For practice, try measuring the coordination angles of the Na⁺ ion (Na130) in 1QIO and its ligands (the side-chain oxygen of Ser72, the main-chain carbonyl oxygen of Ser60, and so on).

docs.title: 3. Behind the measurement display: the atomintr Renderer
docs.text:
The dotted lines and labels of measurements are drawn by a Renderer called atomintr. In the scene tree, an atomintr Renderer named measure is created automatically.

  • The eye icon temporarily hides only the measurement display
  • Select the row and press Delete to remove all measurements at once (can be undone)

Opening the option knob of the Measure group in the tool palette lets you choose the label set to which labels are added. Each set becomes a separate atomintr Renderer, so interactions can be grouped, for example as "active-site distances" or "coordination bonds", and shown, hidden or deleted group by group.

docs.title: 4. Adjust the appearance with a style
docs.text:
Measurement dotted lines are thin lines by default, but they can be switched all at once to a three-dimensional display suited to figures in papers.

  1. Right-click measure (atomintr) in the scene tree
  2. Choose Style > Dashed stick1

The dotted lines change to a dashed three-dimensional display (Dashed stick2 is a preset with a different thickness). To adjust the line thickness or the dash spacing individually, edit the atomintr properties in the inspector (→ atomintr).

docs.title: 5. Delete individual measurements
docs.text:
To remove only a measurement clicked by mistake, delete it from the list instead of deleting the whole Renderer.

  1. Right-click measure (atomintr) in the scene tree and choose Edit interaction list...
  2. A list of the measurements (interactions) belonging to that Renderer is shown
  3. Select the unwanted rows and delete them. The operation can be undone

Differences from CueMol2

In CueMol2, the measurement mode was switched with the ribbon at the top of the window (Measure tab), but in CueMol3 it has moved to the tool palette at the left edge of the molecular view (→ Toolbar and tool palette).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
This is the end of the basic course. From here, follow the task-oriented tutorials to see the actual flow of figure making.

  • Making a protein ribbon figure — basic course on figure making
  • atomintr — settings of the measurement display

Verified against: CueMol3 2.3.8.494

docs.title: Adding, removing and configuring Renderers
docs.text:
This tutorial practices attaching multiple Renderers to one Object to layer the display, and changing settings in the inspector. Continuing from the previous page (Selecting part of a molecule), start with Val2 to Phe3 (A.2:3.*) of lysozyme selected.

Screenshots planned

Screenshots showing the workflow will be added to this page.

docs.title: 1. Add a Renderer to the selection
docs.text:
Display only the two selected residues as ballstick.

  1. In the scene tree, right-click lysozyme and choose New Renderer
  2. Choose ballstick from Renderer type
  3. Selection is already filled with the expression for the current selection (A.2:3.*). Leave it as it is
  4. Renderer name is automatically suggested with an unused name (such as ballstick1). To use a more descriptive name, change it here
  5. Click Create. Only the Val2 to Phe3 part is displayed as ballstick

docs.title: 2. Add a Renderer to the whole molecule
docs.text:
To apply a Renderer to everything regardless of the current selection, uncheck Selection.

  1. Open New Renderer on lysozyme again and choose ribbon
  2. Uncheck Selection
  3. Click Create. The ribbon display is layered over the whole molecule

The simple line drawing, the two-residue ballstick and the whole-molecule ribbon are now stacked. Closing the eye icon of simple1 in the scene tree tidies up the picture and makes it easier to see.

docs.title: 3. Change the displayed range later
docs.text:
Extend the displayed range of ballstick1 from Val2 to Phe3 to Val2 to Glu7.

  1. In the Molecular structure panel, select residues 2 to 7 as a range and click Select (applying the selection expression A.2:7.* in the Selection panel works the same way)
  2. In the scene tree, right-click ballstick1 and choose Change sel > Current

The displayed range of the Renderer is replaced with the current selection and extends to Glu7. Change sel also offers standard ranges such as All (everything), Protein, Water and Ligand.

docs.title: 4. Delete a Renderer
docs.text: Select a row in the scene tree and click the Delete button at the top of the panel. It can also be deleted from the right-click menu. Deletion can be reverted with Undo (Cmd+Z / Ctrl+Z), so feel free to experiment (ballstick1 is kept here).

docs.title: 5. Adjust properties
docs.text:
The fine details of a Renderer's appearance are determined by properties, which are edited in the property inspector on the right (→ Property inspector).

  1. Select ballstick1 in the scene tree
  2. A ballstick-specific section is shown in the Properties tab of the inspector
  3. Set Bond width (thickness of the bond sticks, in Å) and Atom radius (radius of the atom spheres) to 0.4. The model becomes stubby
  4. Enable Show ring to display a plate on the aromatic ring of Phe3

Changes are reflected immediately in the molecular view. There are no OK / Apply buttons; use Undo to revert.

Properties without a type-specific section can all be edited in the Generic tab. Each value has a defined default, and only the items changed from their defaults can be reset (→ Property inspector).

Differences from CueMol2

In CueMol2, properties were edited by opening a dialog for each Renderer and confirmed with OK. In CueMol3, they are edited in the always-visible inspector while watching the result (→ Changes in the interaction model).

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Coloring Renderers — Coloring types and how to color different parts
  • Renderer list — properties of each type in detail

Verified against: CueMol3 2.3.8.494

docs.title: Selecting part of a molecule
docs.text:
In CueMol, to operate on part of a molecule (for example, to change the display style of only that part or to color it), first select that part and then apply the operation. There are several ways to make a selection, and this page practices them together. It uses lysozyme from the previous page (Loading and displaying a structure).

Screenshots planned

Screenshots showing the workflow will be added to this page.

The selected part is highlighted with a semi-transparent overlay in the molecular view.

docs.title: 1. Select by double-clicking
docs.text: Double-clicking an atom in the molecular view selects its residue. Double-clicking another residue adds it to the selection, and double-clicking an already selected residue deselects it.

docs.title: 2. Select from the right-click menu
docs.text:
Right-clicking an atom opens a menu with selection-related items.

Item What is selected Select Atom / Select Residue / Select Chain The clicked atom / residue / chain Select Molecule The whole molecule that was clicked Add Select Atom / Residue / Chain Adds to the selection while keeping the current one Unselect Clears the whole selection Invert Selection Inverts the selection Around / Around Byres The surroundings of the clicked position (3 to 10 Å), by atom / by residue

To select the entire molecule, Select Molecule is the quickest way; to start over with a clean slate, use Unselect.

docs.title: 3. Select in the Molecular structure panel
docs.text:
To choose by residue number or atom name, use the Selection > Molecular structure panel in the left side panel (→ Side panels).

  1. Choose the target molecule (lysozyme) at the top of the panel.
  2. The tree is shown as a chain, residue, atom hierarchy. Select residues Val2 and Phe3 (Cmd / Ctrl + click for multiple selection, Shift + click for range selection).
  3. Click the Select button in the panel to select the corresponding part of the molecule.

Choosing items in the tree does not yet select the molecule. Note that the selection takes effect only after you click Select.

The Center button moves the chosen range to the center of the view, and Zoom centers it and then zooms to fit the size of the range.

docs.title: 4. The Selection panel and the selection builder
docs.text:
The panel dedicated to building selections is the Selection > Selection panel in the left side panel (→ Side panels).

  1. Choose the target molecule (lysozyme) in Molecule.
  2. The Selection field shows the current selection of that molecule as a selection expression. The selection made in the steps so far should already be there as an expression.

Operations in this panel are applied to the molecule's selection immediately and can be undone with Undo.

docs.title: Build a selection with the selection builder
docs.text:
The selection builder below the Selection field lets you build a selection without writing an expression. It has four tabs.

  • Named — applies predefined selections such as protein and water with one click.
  • History — reapplies previously used expressions with a click.
  • Term — creates a single condition such as chain, residue number, or residue name, and combines it with the current selection using Set (replace) / Add (add) / Sub (subtract) / Intsec (intersection). Value candidates are completed automatically from the loaded molecule.
  • Mod — transforms the current selection: Invert / Byres (expand to whole residues) / Sidech / Mainch (side chains / main chains only) / Arnd / Expn (expand to the surroundings within a given distance).

Each button shows the number of atoms that would be selected if it were applied, so you can predict the result as you work. As an experiment, click protein in the Named tab, then click Invert in the Mod tab. The protein selection is inverted, and only the water molecules are selected.

The same selection builder opens from the ▼ button in almost every place where a selection expression is entered, starting with the Selection field of New Renderer. For details on each tab, see Selection builder.

docs.title: Write a selection expression directly
docs.text:
The Selection field can also be edited by hand. For example, the same Val2 to Phe3 as in step 3 is the following expression.

A.2:3.*

It means "all atoms of residues 2 to 3 in chain A". The expression is validated as you type, and a warning is shown if it is invalid. Apply an expression typed by hand with the Select button. Expressions built with the builder also appear in this field as they are, which is a shortcut to learning the syntax (→ Selection expression syntax).

Differences from CueMol2

The hierarchical editor in the CueMol2 selection panel (Hierarchical / Terminal / Around-Expand) has been replaced by the selection builder described above. Its functions are enhanced, for example one-click application of predefined selections and a preview of the atom count.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
The next page uses the selection, so keep Val2 to Phe3 (A.2:3.*) selected.

  • Adding, removing and configuring Renderers — display only the selected part in a different style
  • Selection expression syntax — all the conditions an expression can describe

Verified against: CueMol3 2.3.8.494

docs.title: User interface
docs.text: The CueMol3 main window brings all operating surfaces together in a single window. Unlike CueMol2, no separate windows open for individual functions.

docs.title: Area names
docs.text:
The numbers in the figure correspond to the # column in the table below.

# Area Role Details 1 Toolbar Buttons for frequently used operations (New Tab / file operations / Get PDB / Render / Undo and Redo) Toolbar and tool palette 2 Activity bar The vertical column of icons at the left edge. Switches what the side panel shows (Explorer / View / Selection / Crystal / Actions, etc.). The gear at the bottom opens the Settings tab Side panels 3 Side panel (left) The group of panels for the purpose selected in the activity bar: scene tree, color settings, molecular structure tree, etc. Side panels 4 Tab bar Switches between the open scenes / views and the Settings tab. Tabs can be reordered by dragging 5 Molecular view (MolView) The main 3D display. The viewpoint is moved with the mouse Mouse and trackpad input 6 Tool palette A vertical column of tool buttons floating at the left edge of the molecular view. Switches between the viewpoint / region selection / measurement / bond editing modes Toolbar and tool palette 7 Property inspector (right) Displays and edits the settings of the element selected in the scene tree. Changes are reflected immediately in the molecular view Property inspector 8 Bottom panel Tabs for Console (command line) / Output (log) / Sequence (sequence) / Animation (timeline). Enabling a plugin adds more tabs Bottom panel 9 Status bar Status display. Plugin items (CLI for Console, MCP for MCP Server) are also listed here. The bell at the right end opens the notification center tritium_cli / MCP Server / Notification center — Menu bar Menus such as File / Edit. On macOS it is in the system menu bar at the top of the screen, so it does not appear in the figure. On Windows / Linux it is at the top of the window Menus

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text:
In CueMol3, scenes and views are arranged as tabs.

  • File > New Tab adds a tab for a new scene, or a tab for another view of an existing scene.
  • Tabs can be reordered by dragging.
  • Settings also opens as a tab (only one in the app).
  • The window title is CueMol3 - <scene name>:<view name> and follows the active tab. CueMol3 does not draw a title bar inside the window, so the title is visible only in macOS Mission Control and the Dock, and in the Windows / Linux taskbar and Alt-Tab.

Difference from CueMol2's multiple windows

There is no equivalent of CueMol2's File > New Window. Because the structure shares a single backend, multiple OS windows cannot be opened. Use New Tab instead (→ Merged, renamed and removed features).

docs.title: Showing, hiding and resizing panels
docs.text:
• Clicking the selected icon again in the activity bar closes the side panel. Clicking it again opens the panel.
  • Each panel within the side panel can be collapsed and expanded by clicking its header.
  • Panels can be resized by dragging their borders. The sizes are remembered.

docs.title: The other window
docs.text:
The rendering window, used for ray tracing and movie output, opens as a top-level window independent of the main window. It is modeless, so the molecular view can be manipulated in the main window while it remains open (→ Rendering window).

Windows can be switched from the Window menu (→ Window / Help menu).

Verified against: CueMol3 2.4.0.546

docs.title: Bottom panel
docs.text:
The panel at the bottom of the window has four tabs by default.

Screenshot planned

Tab Contents Console Command line (→ Console) Output Log display Sequence Display and selection of the amino acid / nucleotide sequences of molecules Animation Timeline editing for animations

Enabling a plugin adds the following tab. The Console tab is also part of the Console plugin, and it disappears when the plugin is disabled.

Tab Contents Plugin Trajectory Playback of MD trajectories MD Tools

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Shows the application log. File loading results and error messages appear here.

  • Cmd+A (Edit > Select All) selects the whole log so that it can be copied.

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text: Shows the sequences of the loaded molecules, one grid row per chain. There is no per-molecule switching; the chains of all molecules in the scene are listed together.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text: Operation Action Click Toggles the selection of that residue and moves the molecular view to the position of that residue Drag Toggles the selection of the residues from the start point to the end point Shift + click Selects from the most recently marked position to the clicked position Right-click Opens the menu described below

docs.title: Right-click menu
docs.text:
Item Action Toggle sel Toggles the selection of that residue Around 3 / 5 / 7 / 10 Selects atoms within the given distance of the selection Around Byresid 3 / 5 / 7 / 10 Same as above, but selects whole residues Unselect all Clears the selection Invert sel Inverts the selection Copy sequence Copies the sequence to the clipboard in one-letter code (residues without a one-letter code become *) Center here Brings that residue to the center of the molecular view

The boundary between the name column on the left and the sequence grid can be dragged to change the column width.

Known issue: selection updates are delayed

After the selection is changed, the highlight in the molecular view may take about 0.5 seconds to update. This is a known issue under investigation.

docs.title: Animation
docs.text:
Edits the animation timeline. It uses a strip layout like Blender's, with each animation element shown as one strip.

  • Drag a strip to move its start position, or drag its edge to change its length.
  • Strips can be added, deleted and reordered.
  • The play button plays the animation in the molecular view.
  • The current time display is editable. Type a time and press Enter to jump to that point (→ Entering times).
  • Selecting a strip shows the detailed settings of that element in the inspector on the right (type-specific settings and the generic property list).
  • The start camera can be chosen in the timeline header.
  • An element whose start-time reference (Relative to) cannot be resolved is shown with diagonal stripes and cannot be played until this is fixed.

To export the created animation as a movie file, use Rendering > Movie rendering... (→ Rendering window).

Note

While animation properties are being edited, the molecular view does not follow in real time. Play the animation to check the result.

docs.title: Console
docs.text:
A command line for running CueMol operations as commands. Switching to PyMOL compatibility mode on the toolbar allows PyMOL commands such as fetch 1crn to be typed as they are.

This tab is part of the Console plugin, which is enabled by default (→ Console). It is the first tab of the bottom panel and stays in front until another tab is selected.

docs.title: Trajectory
docs.text:
Plays MD trajectories loaded with File > Open MD Trajectory.... Frame blocks are shown on the timeline, with playback, frame stepping and seeking.

This tab is part of the MD Tools plugin, which is disabled by default. Enable it in Settings > Plugins > Installed (→ Plugins).

Verified against: CueMol3 2.4.0.546

docs.title: Property inspector
docs.text:
The property inspector on the right side of the window is a permanent panel that shows and edits the settings of the element selected in the scene tree. It replaces the various property dialogs of CueMol2.

Screenshot planned

docs.title: Differences from CueMol2
docs.text:
CueMol2 CueMol3 Form A modal dialog for each Renderer type A single permanent panel Molecular view The dialog hides it / blocks interaction Always visible and interactive When changes take effect When OK / Apply is pressed The moment a value is changed Reverting Cancel Undo (Cmd+Z)

Because edits take effect immediately, there are no OK / Cancel buttons. Use Undo to revert a change.

docs.title: Switching the view
docs.text:
Selecting an element in the scene tree, or double-clicking it, shows its contents in the inspector. The tabs at the top of the inspector switch the view.

Tab Contents Properties A settings view organized by purpose. It is divided into sections, which are opened one at a time (only the scene shows all sections open side by side) Generic A general-purpose editor that lists all the properties of the element

The tab that opens by default depends on the type of the selected element.

docs.title: Renderer
docs.text:
The Properties tab shows a Common section (basic settings and edge lines). Opacity, material, edge line settings and so on are adjusted here. For Renderers without faces (simple / trace / spline / contour, etc.), the edge line settings are not shown (→ Edge lines).

Detailed settings for each Renderer type

Settings specific to a Renderer type (ribbon / ballstick / molsurf, etc.) are shown in a dedicated section for each type. Nested properties that do not appear there (such as the cross-section shape of cartoon) can be edited in the Generic tab.

docs.title: Renderer group
docs.text: Only Name / Visible / Locked are shown. Items that have no meaning for a group (opacity, material, edge lines) are not shown.

docs.title: Object
docs.text: Name / Selection / Visible / Locked / Linked (read-only) can be edited. A density map (DensityMap) also shows a Density map section for handling the map type (Map type / Effective kind) (→ DensityMap).

docs.title: Scene
docs.text: Opened from Properties... in the Scene menu. It has settings for ambient occlusion / anti-aliasing / background / color proofing (→ Scene reference). Because there are few items, the sections are not collapsed and are all displayed.

docs.title: View
docs.text: Opened from View property... in the View menu. It is shown in the Generic tab.

docs.title: Entering numbers
docs.text:
A numeric setting field can be changed in three ways.

  • Pressing the left or right arrow increases or decreases the value one step at a time (holding the button repeats the step).
  • Dragging left or right over the number changes it continuously. Dragging about 3/4 of the field width covers the full range of allowed values from end to end. Holding Shift makes the change finer, and holding Ctrl / Cmd makes it coarser. Pressing Esc restores the value from before the drag started.
  • Clicking the number turns it into a direct-entry field; confirm with Enter (cancel with Esc). Values outside the allowed range are clamped into the range.

The polygon subdivision settings (Detail / Axial detail / Section detail) are not numeric input fields but drop-downs offering a set of levels. What is visible is the difference between 4 and 8, not between 8 and 9, hence this form. The levels are basically powers of 2 (2 / 4 / 8 / 16 / 32), but only the Detail of dsurface also offers 1 and 24. The list also includes the current value and the default value.

The selection builder can also be opened from the Selection field. The number of atoms shown beside the apply button is also displayed here.

docs.title: Entering times
docs.text:
The Start time / Duration of an animation element, time values in the Generic tab, and the current time of the Animation panel are displayed as a timecode in M:SS.mmm format (H:MM:SS.mmm for one hour or more), and are edited segment by segment.

  • Click a segment to select it, then drag left or right to increase or decrease it in that unit. Holding Shift makes the step 1/10 as fine, and holding Ctrl / Cmd makes it 10 times larger.
  • Up / Down increase or decrease the selected segment one step at a time. Left / Right move between segments.
  • Typing digits overwrites the selected segment (typing 75 in the seconds segment carries over to 1:15).
  • Enter or a double-click opens an expression field, where a timecode such as 1:30.500, a value with a unit such as 250ms / 1.5s, or a relative value such as +2s can be entered. Esc cancels.

For Start time / Duration in the inspector, the timeline strip follows the drag, and releasing the mouse button counts as a single Undo.

docs.title: Generic tab
docs.text:
Shows the properties of the element as a list of names and values.

  • String / integer / real / boolean / enum values can be edited.
  • A color can be chosen either as a named color of the scene or as a color relative to the molecule. A vector is edited component by component (x / y / z / w), and a time with a timecode input field (→ Entering times).
  • Nested properties are also expanded as dot-separated keys and can be edited.
  • A number is committed when focus leaves the input field or Enter is pressed. Retyping a number can still be reverted with a single Undo.
  • Each item can be reset to its default value. Reset all to default resets everything at once (a confirmation is shown; properties that no longer exist are skipped). The name (name) and the selection (sel) are exceptions: neither method resets them to their default values.
  • Changes can be undone.

Verified against: CueMol3 2.3.21.544

docs.title: Mouse and trackpad input
docs.text: This page describes how to manipulate the view in the molecular view, and how the object under the pointer is handled.

docs.title: Default operations
docs.text:
These are the operations when the Navigate tool (the default) is selected in the tool palette.

Operation Action Left drag Rotate Wheel Zoom

Change from CueMol2: the wheel zooms

For a while during the migration, the wheel was assigned to translation. It has now been restored to wheel = zoom.

docs.title: Pointing device setting
docs.text:
Mice and trackpads call for opposite behavior from scrolling (a mouse wheel should zoom, but a two-finger scroll on a trackpad should translate). In CueMol3, specify which to use with Settings > Input > Pointing device.

Setting Behavior Auto-detect (default) Automatically determines whether the device is a mouse or a trackpad from the characteristics of the scrolling Mouse The wheel zooms Mac trackpad Two-finger scroll translates; pinch zooms

Auto-detection is an estimate

The OS provides no way to know the device type, so Auto-detect is an estimate based on the characteristics of scroll events (whether there is a horizontal component, whether values are integers or fractions, whether pinch or rotate gestures occur, and so on). A mouse with a high-resolution wheel may be judged to be a trackpad, or the reverse. In that case, select Mouse / Mac trackpad explicitly. The detection result is shown in the settings screen.

docs.title: Sensitivity and precision settings
docs.text:
Settings > Input > Mouse & Navigation has the following settings.

Setting Description Pointing device The pointing device type described above XY Rotation Sensitivity Sensitivity of rotation around the X / Y axes (0.1 to 5.0) Pick Precision Tolerance radius when picking an atom or Object by clicking (pixels, 1 to 50) GPU Picking Hit-testing method (see below) Hover Info Display of what is under the pointer (see below) Hover Highlight Highlighting of what is under the pointer (see below)

docs.title: Picking and hover display
docs.text: This section explains how CueMol determines the object the pointer is pointing at in the molecular view, and how it shows it.

docs.title: Hits match the drawn shape
docs.text:
Click hit-testing is performed against the shape the Renderer actually drew. The same shape that was drawn is redrawn on the GPU, and the element that owns the pixel under the pointer is read back. With cartoon / ribbon / tube, clicking anywhere on the band hits that residue.

Hit-testing method Targets Drawn shape cartoon / tube / ribbon / spline / nucl / trace / tracestick / cpk / anisou / ballstick / simple / dsurface Atom position Molecules generated by symmetry operations (symm)

dsurface (a molecular surface computed directly from the molecule) is a target only when the drawing mode is Fill. The atom that owns the point on the surface is picked, and the faces around that atom are highlighted. Wireframe and Dots are not targets (→ dsurface).

Only dsurface is a target; molsurf is not. A molecular surface generated with Tools > Mol surface generation... is created as an Object (MolSurfObj) separate from the molecule (MolCoord), and molsurf, which draws it, is a Renderer that targets that surface Object, not the molecule. Even if the shapes look the same, the molecule's atoms cannot be traced from a point on the surface (→ MolSurfObj).

Labels and atomic interactions (atomintr) are not click targets either.

Hit-testing used to rely on atom positions only

Previously, the Renderer registered one point per atom (for backbone-type Renderers such as cartoon, one per residue, at the CA position) and the one nearest the pointer was searched for. As a result, the center of a wide ribbon was treated as "nothing there", and it could be picked only by aiming near the CA.

Rectangle selection and lasso selection still use atom-position hit-testing. How to enclose items in cartoon and similar Renderers is unchanged (→ Toolbar and tool palette).

Anything farther back than the position where it fades out of sight in fog is no longer picked. Previously, clicking where nothing was visible could hit a shape behind.

The value of Pick Precision is used as the search range around the pointer in both methods.

docs.title: Showing what is under the pointer
docs.text:
When the pointer moves over the molecular view, what is under it is shown in a small chip at the lower left.

  • The first line shows a chain-name badge and the residue (ALA 10). For atom-level Renderers, the atom name follows (ALA 10 CA). cartoon / ribbon / tube / spline / nucl / trace have bands that represent residues, so no atom name is shown (the same applies to tracestick).
  • The second line shows the Object and Renderer the element belongs to (1crn | cartoon1). For a molecule generated by symmetry operations, the name of the symmetry operation follows.

The chip is transparent to clicks, so it does not interfere with operating on what is under it.
